title: A father's scent helps babies synchronize their brains with new adults
author: Karina Petrova
summary: Karina Petrova reports on a Science Advances study by Yaara Endevelt-Shapira, Linoy Schwartz and Ruth Feldman on how a father's body odor affects infant social brain activity. Using dual EEG with 40 infants aged five to twelve months, the researchers found infants showed higher interbrain synchrony with their fathers than with a stranger, in the alpha frequency band. When a t-shirt carrying the father's scent was placed near the infant during play with an unfamiliar man, the infant's neural synchrony with the stranger rose to a level not significantly different from that with the father, and positive arousal such as smiling increased. The effect was larger for infants whose fathers reported more daily childcare involvement. The article lists caveats, including a small sample, wide age range, a blank-shirt control and possible habituation, and notes caregiving styles do not strictly follow biological sex.
points: A father's scent alone can increase an infant's brain synchrony with a stranger, effectively invoking his presence.
Infants synchronized more strongly with their own fathers than with an unfamiliar man, specifically in the alpha band linked to attention and social processing.
The scent also raised positive arousal behaviors such as smiling, laughing and cooing during interaction with the stranger.
The boost was largest for infants whose fathers were more involved in daily care, linking everyday presence to the infant's social openness.
Limitations include 40 infants, a wide age range, a blank-shirt control that cannot rule out general human scent, and possible olfactory habituation.
quotes: By simply smelling their father’s body odor, infants essentially invoke his presence, allowing them to form stronger neural connections with strangers.
Fathers often engage in more high-energy play, which stimulates positive arousal and encourages infants to explore their surroundings.
The researchers conducted a small study involving 40 infants, aged five to twelve months, and their biological fathers.
The infants displayed higher interbrain synchrony with their own fathers than with the stranger.
When the father’s scent was present, the neural synchrony between the infant and the stranger increased.
During the sessions with the stranger, the presence of the father’s scent elevated the infant’s positive arousal.

The researchers also surveyed the fathers about their routine involvement in childcare at home. Infants of fathers who reported higher levels of daily involvement showed a more pronounced increase in neural synchrony when exposed to the paternal odor.

The experimental design compared the father’s scent to a blank shirt. This leaves open the possibility that infants were reacting to a general human scent rather than their specific father’s odor, though the stranger’s own scent was present during both conditions.
